webTitle: California announces minimum wage increase as governor taunts Trump

fields.headline: California announces minimum wage increase as governor taunts Trump
fields.trailText: Gavin Newsom says new pay floor of $17.40, set to become highest of any US state, will go into effect on 1 January
fields.bodyText: Governor Gavin Newsom of California announced that the state’s minimum wage will rise to $17.40 next year, a pay floor set to become the highest of any US state. The pay bump will go into effect starting 1 January, Newsom announced on Friday. The state’s current minimum rate is $16.90. In a news release, Newsom touted the move as a salve for working families amid high living costs and took a jab at the Trump administration. “For years, Donald Trump and Republicans have blocked efforts to raise the federal minimum wage while handing tax breaks to billionaires and big corporations,” Newsom said. The federal minimum wage was last increased during George W Bush’s presidency, when it rose from $6.55 to $7.25. Opponents of a federal increase fear adverse effects to the labor market such as job losses. “California has chosen a different path – one that rewards work, grows the economy and puts working families first. We believe if you work hard, you deserve a decent paycheck. They think $7.25 an hour is enough. We don’t,” Newsom said. Thirty states in addition to Washington DC have set wage rates above the federal minimum. The state of Washington will trail close behind California in 2027 with a minimum wage of $17.13, according to data from the Department of Labor. In New York City and three nearby counties, the minimum wage is $17. Since Newsom took the gubernatorial seat in 2019, the state’s minimum wage has grown from $12, according to his office. Still, for a family of two working adults and two children in California, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) estimate each adult must earn $36.38 to cover food, childcare, healthcare, housing and transportation, among other basic necessities. Cost-of-living concerns have been at the forefront of the upcoming midterm elections. The Trump administration has faced blowback over the protracted war with Iran that has led to a surge in gas prices across the nation. In California, a state that relies on a reduced emission type of gasoline, fuel prices topped $6 a gallon in recent months.

webTitle: Upheaval in Maine and another 100-day campaign – can Democrats pull it off?

fields.headline: Upheaval in Maine and another 100-day campaign – can Democrats pull it off?
fields.trailText: Troy Jackson gained the party nomination for Senate, but now he needs to consolidate support to take on Susan Collins
fields.bodyText: Troy Jackson is ready to move on. In fewer than 100 days, the new Democratic nominee has to convince Maine voters to send him to the US Senate – and he’s trying to do it without dwelling on Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race after accusations of rape, which he denies. “The movement represented in this room did not just begin two weeks ago,” said Jackson, a progressive lumberjack and former state lawmaker who won nearly all the delegates at a hastily organized special convention last Saturday. “I’ve always known that your trust has to be earned.” On stage, no one mentioned Platner by name, but the fallout from the oyster farmer’s campaign collapse hung over the room. He had ridden an anti‑establishment wave before crashing under a series of scandals – which included problematic online posts, a tattoo resembling a Nazi symbol and allegations of abusive behavior in past relationships. Jackson, who previously launched an unsuccessful bid for governor this year, now faces a compressed timeline to build the same momentum his predecessor generated against Susan Collins, the moderate Republican who has weathered every challenger during her three decades in the Senate. Maine is central to Democrats’ effort to pick up the four seats they need to regain control of the upper chamber in the midterms. But some in the party worry that Jackson faces a steep climb in a short window. “He won an interparty fight – which is nothing like the fight he’s got ahead of him,” said Lynn Bromley, a former Democratic state senator. “He’s going to have to build a statewide coalition. That’s a whole different process.” “I would say Jackson has momentum, but I would also say momentum isn’t the same thing as trust,” she added. Who Jackson needs to win Jackson quickly emerged as the natural heir to Platner’s anti‑oligarchy message. More than 17,000 voters turned out for the county‑level delegate elections, and by the time the roughly 500 selected delegates arrived in Bangor, most had already pledged to support Jackson. In a Tuesday interview on political talkshow Morning Joe, Jackson acknowledged that Platner was the more compelling orator, but said his focus now is making sure voters understand the election is about “the movement”, not any one candidate. To win in November, he still has to consolidate Democratic support and reach voters outside Platner’s core supporters. The most crucial demographic for Jackson is 2020 ticket‑splitters in Maine – those who backed Susan Collins for Senate and Joe Biden for president. Back then, Collins ultimately won by nine points, defeating Democrat Sara Gideon, the former state house speaker, despite trailing in most public polls. A Guardian review shows that more municipalities voted for both Biden and Collins than they did for a straight Democratic ticket that year. One of those voters is Wendy Tooth, a physiotherapist in Manchester, who’s been “disappointed” with Collins since her 2020 vote for the incumbent, and particularly since Donald Trump’s re-election. “I wasn’t really a Graham Platner fan,” Tooth, 58, said. “[Collins] doesn’t seem as centrist as she used to be. She seems to go along with a lot of Trump’s policies, which I don’t agree with.” Part of the unenrolled bloc that makes up about a third of voters in the Pine Tree state, Tooth says she needs to see Jackson “work across party lines” – and Collins take firmer positions against the war in Iran and the deadly federal immigration crackdown across the country – before making her decision. Democrats such as Alan Blake of Thomaston say the party must now rally behind Jackson regardless of any concerns about the chaos that has plagued the race so far. “We’re just going to carry Jackson in there because we absolutely need the policies he stands for,” Blake, 74, added. “It’s not drastic to say we’re trying to save democracy here.” And Ellie Gunnoe, 39, a psychiatric nurse practitioner and registered Democrat in New Gloucester, said Jackson – a fifth‑generation logger from Aroostook county – can reach voters across the state as a “working‑class Mainer”. “We just need someone fighting in our corner,” Gunnoe added, noting that the fatal shooting of 26-year-old Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, by an ICE agent in Biddeford, is one of the key motivators pushing her to the ballot box this year. “My husband is Mexican American and is the exact same age and brown, and so it’s just been feeling increasingly unsafe for people like us,” she added. A slice of moderate Democrats who voted for Janet Mills, Maine’s term-limited governor, in the June primary – after she had suspended her campaign but remained on the ballot – are also in play. One of them, Brenda Garrand, 69, of Rockland, said she plans to vote for Jackson even though she doesn’t consider herself a progressive. “I don’t think he’s the best and brightest, I don’t think he is Senate material,” she said. “But we’ve got to have a Senate majority.” Mills, for her part, told a local ABC affiliate this week that Collins is “vulnerable” and “should be defeated”, but did not endorse Jackson directly. Jackson’s run could be buoyed by the anti-Trump animus that’s grown since the financial fallout of the ongoing war. According to a recent New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll, only 39% of likely Maine voters approved of the president’s job performance since he returned to the White House. “Susan Collins keeps telling us everything is just fine. And you know they act like you know we’re idiots. We know it isn’t. We all have eyes,” Jackson said in Bangor. He used his victory to highlight Collins’ votes to confirm the supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh and advance the president’s $70bn bill to guarantee funding for federal immigration enforcement. “Who has she served?” Jackson asked the audience. “She has served Donald Trump. She voted with them 96% of the time.” Meanwhile, Collins has sought to brand Jackson a “Bernie bro”, pointing to his long relationship with Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, and his role leading Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign in Maine. Ronald Schmidt, a politics professor at the University of Southern Maine, said that attack puts the onus on Jackson to “flip that playbook” of being affiliated with an outsider and “link [Collins] to Trump”. But some local Republicans counter that Jackson’s more than two decades as a state legislator, and a failed run for Congress in 2014, mean he lacks Platner’s outsider profile. “He is Maine’s establishment,” said Chuck Ellis, chair of the Cumberland county GOP. “All the appeal of Platner being anti‑establishment is lost when you replace him with a career politician.” The long road ahead, paved with attack ads An ad offensive from conservative Pacs has begun painting Jackson as an extension of Platner, often using footage from their time on the campaign trail when they endorsed each other. After Jackson clinched the nomination on Saturday, the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) even pushed out an AI video of Platner morphing into Jackson with the caption: “No tattoo, same crazy.” James Blair, a former White House adviser now leading Trump’s midterm operation, wrote that Jackson carried “all the baggage” of Platner “without the ‘rizz”. And the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) – the top Senate GOP Super Pac, which has pledged more than $40m to the race – is highlighting the many scandals that plagued the unvetted Platner, alongside reporting about Jackson’s alleged fiery temper during his time in the state legislature. “Jackson is like Graham Platner but worse,” the voiceover in a video says. Meanwhile, the Republican National Committee (RNC) quickly cast Jackson’s nomination as illegitimate, drawing a parallel to the 2024 Democratic convention, where Harris became the nominee after delegates originally pledged to Biden backed her following his withdrawal from the race. “This coronation is proof that Democrats are willing to shove socialism down the throats of Maine voters,” spokesperson Kristen Cianci said. Collins told reporters in Casco last weekend that her challenger’s platform economic populism – which includes many of Platner’s policies such as Medicare for All and taxing the ultra-wealthy – is untenable. “It is disturbing for me to hear Troy say that everything should be free, when in fact it’s going to be middle- and low-income taxpayers who are going to be paying the bill,” she said. Jackson’s ground game is also in need of a significant financial boost to compete with Collins’ war chest of more than $11m cash on hand, according to her latest disclosures. As of now, Jackson’s campaign reports he has amassed $2m since he won the nomination. That’s on top of the $1m he raised since he formally entered the Senate race in early July. Perhaps more daunting than the attacks or the finances, however, is the support Collins has built over five terms, and a record of political survival that has been impossible to beat – even when the odds appear to be against her. “She’s an intimidating political presence, and I think people underestimate that,” said Matt Gorman, a Republican strategist. Collins has spent much of the race, and the years leading up to it, underscoring the millions of dollars in federal funding she’s steered to Maine as chair of the powerful Senate appropriations committee. Her campaign spokesperson, Shawn McRoderick, said the senator looks forward to “waging a vigorous, issues‑oriented campaign that will distinguish her record of accomplishment against Troy’s angry soundbites”. In a small state, tangible results are hard to ignore. “I was speaking to a town official from upstate who was able to get fire department money to improve the local volunteer fire department with the help of Collins’ office,” Schmidt recalled. “People who’ve directly been helped by her staff probably will vote for her again in this election, regardless of their party ID.” While antipathy toward the gerontocracy may color many midterm races this year, Collins’ seniority in Congress – despite serving alongside an administration many Mainers can’t stomach – may be her strongest asset. “With Collins you actually have serious influence that can successfully make progress at cooling off the Trump administration when she feels like that’s necessary and that’s appropriate,” said Ellis. “To lose that, you would have to be able to say that we have a substantial upgrade that’s going to do so much better for us.” Andrew Witherspoon contributed reporting

webTitle: Trump’s favorite cable news channel is pushing back against his war on Iran

fields.headline: Trump’s favorite cable news channel is pushing back against his war on Iran
fields.trailText: Prominent Fox News hosts have expressed concern, bewilderment and frustration over US objectives in Iran
fields.bodyText: Throughout his two presidencies, Donald Trump has leaned on reliable support from the conservative opinion wing of his favorite cable news channel, Fox News. But, like a broad swathe of the American public, several traditionally supportive commentators on the channel have recently expressed concerns about whether the war on Iran is succeeding, suggesting that Trump is on increasingly dicey footing in the conservative media world he relies on for backing. While he isn’t close to losing the support of hosts such as Sean Hannity or Jesse Watters, Trump has received scrutiny from one of the network’s top personalities, Laura Ingraham, who has regularly questioned whether the US has achieved the tactical wins it has claimed in Iran. He has also faced reliable skepticism from one of the network’s most prominent commentators about the armed forces, Johnny “Joey” Jones, a contributor and retired Marine Corps staff sergeant who lost both his legs in combat in Afghanistan. Jones’ commentary is particularly salient because he is close to Pete Hegseth, his former Fox colleague who is now the defense secretary and who oversaw Jones’ recent re-enlistment in the Marine Corps reserve. That’s not to mention the network’s military commentators, such as retired Lt Gen Keith Kellogg, who said on Fox on Wednesday that Trump needs to “change” his strategy. “I don’t think we’re close, in that regard of finishing the job, if we are just depending on bombing,” said Kellogg, who left his perch at Fox for a short-lived stint in Trump’s second administration as his envoy focused on Ukraine. “Bombing is not going to get the job done.” On her 24 July show, Ingraham acknowledged a New York Times report that Trump faced threats that forced him to use an alternative plane to Air Force One and suggested claims that the US has demolished Iran’s military seem inaccurate. “If Iran can credibly threaten Air Force One overseas, we didn’t decimate their military capabilities, obviously,” she said. “They’re still capable of a lot of harm.” She made a similar point in June, telling viewers: “We keep hearing their military is destroyed. But if they’re destroyed, how are they continuing to hit us?” Back in March, Ingraham called for the US to precipitously investigate and “address head-on” what she called a “horrible unintended tragedy of this war”, the killing of 175 civilians – mostly children – in an errant attack on a school in Iran. Later that month, Ingraham questioned whether Trump understood the “complexity” of the war in Iran, suggesting that he had not properly been briefed. “Was the president fully briefed about the risks of all of this from the beginning?” she asked on 30 March. “And was he then able to take it all in and understand the complexity of this, how complex it could actually get, and further possibilities of casualties or other damage, the difficulty of dealing with these people? Or was he told this would be relatively quick in and out?” From the beginning of the war, Jones on his weekend show sought to emphasize the stakes of the conflict after multiple American service-members were killed in a counter-attack in Kuwait. “It’s important and it’s okay for any Americans who are saying: ‘Wait just a minute. Tell me more. Tell me why we are at war. Explain to me why this was imminent,’” he said. “I don’t think that questions your patronage to the American government or even if you’re Maga or what have you. It doesn’t question president Trump’s wisdom in this.” On 18 July, after reports that two American service members had been killed in Jordan, he questioned whether the US strategy was working. “I often say that president Trump [should] speak loudly and carry a big stick,” he said on air. “Right now might be the time that the big stick part of it matters most, because simply dropping bombs from the air isn’t stopping them from doing what they want to do.” While he mentioned some potential options the US could take, he noted that they would take time, “and time is not on our side”. A few days later, Brit Hume, a Fox News analyst, connected the quagmire to Trump’s political promises to voters. “He promised to keep us out of endless wars or unsatisfactory wars, and now he’s in one, and it’s not at all clear how it’s gonna end. So, he’s vulnerable on this point, and in political terms, he does need to get this over with.” In June, John Roberts, a Fox News anchor, said he was “a little puzzled” about Trump’s Iran negotiation strategy. Even Watters, a reliable Trump booster, seemed skeptical about his ever-changing timelines for reaching a deal with Iran to end the war. “He keeps saying: ‘We’re very close. We’re days away.’ And I don’t know what that means. We’ve heard that for a very long time,” he said in June. Hosts on the network’s business channel have also regularly questioned the rising price of oil and the impact on American consumers, particularly ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. As Stuart Varney, a Fox Business Network anchor, put it in March: “Houston, we have a problem.”

webTitle: Justice department admits reflecting pool damage not caused by vandals as it moves to drop charges against Olympian – as it happened

fields.headline: Justice department admits reflecting pool damage not caused by vandals as it moves to drop charges against Olympian – as it happened
fields.trailText: US attorney in Washington DC moves to dismiss charges against David Hearn, telling court that documents indicated ‘damage was the result of flawed installation’
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second TRump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: Kamala Harris, speaking at the National Urban League conference in Nashville, said that she has “not made a decision” on a potential 2028 presidential run. The US government released its anxiously awaited plan for how to manage the Colorado river crisis on Friday, outlining cuts in water supplied to California, Arizona and Nevada. During a cabinet meeting at Camp David, the US treasury secretary Scott Bessent carelessly revealed plans for the US to buy $5-$10bn ⁠in Japanese yen in a scribbled ‘to do’ list left visible to a Reuters photographer. The Financial Times reported later that the Federal Reserve Bank of New York sold euros to buy yen on behalf of the US treasury department to ⁠support the Japanese currency. In a court filing, the office of the US attorney in Washington DC, Jeanine Pirro, moved to dismiss charges against David Hearn, a former Olympian her office had accused on vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, Pirro’s office said documents on the renovation indicate that damage “was the result of flawed installation by the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings … and the rush to complete the project”. Donald Trump told reporters he wasn’t sure whether he should grant Patriot missiles to Ukraine as he said he would, because “they can someday turn on you”. The US treasury department intervened in ⁠yen exchange ⁠rates on Friday to ⁠support the Japanese currency through outright ⁠purchases, the ‌Financial ‌Times reported. According to the report, citing unnamed sources, the Federal Reserve Bank ‌of New York conducted a sale of euros to buy ⁠yen on behalf of the Department of the Treasury. The depreciation of the yen, which dipped last week to its weakest level since 1986, has been driven by a number of factors, including rising oil prices, according to Bloomberg News. During a cabinet meeting at Camp David on Friday, the US treasury secretary Scott Bessent carelessly revealed plans for the US to buy $5-$10bn ⁠in Japanese yen in a scribbled ‘to do’ list left visible to a Reuters photographer. The image, taken over Bessent’s shoulder during a portion of the meeting open to journalists, showed a Camp David notepad with the underscored words “To Do” followed by “Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil.” Bessent’s name card on the Camp David conference table is visible and positioned immediately above the notepad. The ‌photograph was taken at ‌11:33 am local time, Reuters reported. Video of the televised portion of the cabinet meeting showed that the notepad was still clearly visible in front of Bessent when he spoke, to praise the president, 30 minutes later. A treasury spokesperson did not immediately respond to a Reuters request ‌for comment on the contents of the notepad, “or whether the Treasury had intervened to help prop up the yen’s value against the dollar on Friday,” the news agency said. Earlier on Friday, about two hours before the note was seen in front of Bessent, Reuters reported that the treasury department had notified a number of banks that ‌it could intervene in the yen market that day, an unnamed source said. Japanese authorities had stepped in to prop up the yen earlier on Friday, triggering a substantial strengthening of the Japanese currency during early trading hours. In a court filing on Friday, the office of the US attorney in Washington DC, Jeanine Pirro, moved to dismiss charges against David Hearn, a former Olympian her office had accused on vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. In asking to dismiss the criminal indictment, Pirro’s office told the DC Superior Court that “it was not until after the return of the indictment,” that the Department of the Interior “provided additional documents” to prosecutors “indicating that damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in June 2026 was the result of flawed installation by the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings (“AIC”), and the rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America 250 celebration in the weeks surrounding Independence Day 2026.” “It was not until after these documents were produced,” Pirro’s office added, that her office “first became aware of information showing that the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism as initially represented by DOI.” “The Trump administration’s case against Davey Hearn should never have been brought,” Hearn’s lawyers, Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann and Steve Levin said in a statement. “Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong. The government’s approach was ready, fire, aim. The administration owes Mr. Hearn an apology.” The government’s request to dismiss the case against Hearn said that when Pirro inspected the pool on 17 July, “as a defense expert inspected the now-drained Reflecting Pool” that she “immediately noted extensive damage throughout” the pool and requested “all records regarding the installation of the lining.” “These documents indicated a rushed and flawed installation process, with repeated failures of the lining during the installation process, and extensive peeling of the lining throughout the Reflecting Pool,” the filing added. In a social media post sent from Air Force One on Friday afternoon, Donald Trump drew attention to video of tens of thousands of migrants entering the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco the day before. “What’s happening with Spain,” Trump wrote, characterizing the arrival of migrants in the enclave on the North African coast that has been a Spanish possession since 1580 as an invasion, “happened in the United States during the Sleepy Joe Biden Administration, and it will happen again, only worse, if the Dumocrats ever again gain power.” Trump illustrated his warning about the US-Mexico border with video of migrants crossing the border from Morocco into the Spanish territory that Morocco claims as its own, and calls “occupied”. This is not the first time that Trump has sought to sow fear about the US southern border by using video of migrants in Europe. In January 2016, Trump released an ad in support of his first presidential campaign that featured images of migrants surging across a border fence as a narrator promised that Trump would “stop illegal immigration by building a wall on our southern border that Mexico will pay for”. That video, however, was not recorded on the US-Mexico border, but in another Spanish enclave on the Moroccan coast, Melilla, in 2014. Trump’s closing ad for that campaign, released in November 2016 also featured footage of migrants in Europe, passed off as video of immigrants streaming across the border from Mexico into the United States. Near the start of that ad, as the candidate could be heard complaining of “massive illegal immigration,” thousands of people were shown walking along a highway. As I reported in 2016, however, that video was not shot along the southern border of the US — where Trump had promised to build a great wall — but in Hungary, at the height of the 2105 migrant crisis, and it showed Syrian refugees, desperate for safe passage to Germany, marching out of Budapest. That video was lifted, without permission, from a social media account of Nabih Bulos, a foreign correspondent who had accompanied the refugees. “When this footage was taken, thousands of refugees were on an odyssey through the Balkan corridor and Europe to escape the cataclysm ripping their country apart,” Bulos told me at the time. “As a son of two Palestinian refugees who benefited from Jordan’s largesse, a naturalized American welcomed to the country even after 9/11, as well as a working conflict journalist, the last thing I would want this footage to be used for is to embody Trump’s xenophobic, repugnant message.” Earlier this year, the Republican-led House appropriations committee referred to the dispute over the two enclaves in a report, in which it noted “that the Spanish-administered cities of Ceuta and Melilla are located in Moroccan territory and remain the subject of Morocco’s longstanding claim.” The committee added that it “supports efforts by the Secretary of State to encourage diplomatic engagement between Morocco and Spain on the future status of Ceuta and Melilla.” The US government released its anxiously awaited plan for how to manage the Colorado river crisis on Friday, outlining cuts in water supplied to California, Arizona and Nevada. The proposal from the US Bureau of Reclamation spares Colorado, Utah, New Mexico and Wyoming from facing mandatory cuts, for now. But it is a temporary fix as the states that rely on the river continue to fight over a long-term management plan for the dwindling resource that supplies huge swaths of the western US. The proposal is the federal government’s answer to a years-long stalemate between the seven states responsible for forming a plan on how to distribute the deep cuts needed to pull the system back from the brink. It comes just months before the framework that currently governs the essential and imperiled waterway is set to expire. “This framework provides the flexibility to respond to changing hydrologic conditions while preserving the opportunity for the Basin States to continue working toward durable, consensus-based solutions,” said Doug Burgum, the US interior secretary, in a press release. Under the 10-year plan, the Lower Basin states could face deep cuts of up to 3m acre-feet (3.7bn kiloliters) a year – up to 40% of their collective total – “subject to hydrology”, according to the press release by the Department of the Interior. That’s about enough water annually to serve more than 25 million people. The plan would also allow annual releases of between 5m and 12m acre-feet from Lake Powell, the basin’s second-largest reservoir. Under the 10-year federal framework, water management decisions will be made every two years. The federal government is expected to release a record of decision in the coming week that will detail operations under the plan in the short term, but it is likely they will closely follow a proposal issued by the lower basin states earlier this year that would shave 3.2m acre-feet from their combined total over 2027 and 2028. Senior Democrats accused Republicans in the US Congress of becoming “gelatinous blobs” who won’t stand up to Donald Trump and “rubber stamps” for his war on Iran. Elizabeth Warren, a US senator for Massachusetts, and Chris Van Hollen, a US senator for Maryland, argued that the Republican-controlled Congress had surrendered its constitutional authority to the president. In interviews with the Guardian, the senators urged their Republican colleagues to stand with Democrats and assert Congress’s authority as a separate branch of the federal government – with power over declaring war. “The Republicans have all had their spines surgically removed,” Warren said in Michigan, while stumping for the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. “I mean, they’re just gelatinous blobs that kind of make it through the United States Senate.” The constitution sets up three separate branches of government to hold one another accountable, Warren noted – and the assumption was that each of the three branches would “jealously guard its own powers”. Current and former prosecutors are denouncing the Trump administration for fast-tracking the deportation of immigrant children, as a key contract for legal services is set to expire on Friday. A series of federal laws has for decades shielded child immigrants from removal, either to protect their safety or to allow them to testify against abusers or human traffickers. But the Trump administration has undermined those laws, immigrant advocates and prosecutors say, by directing immigration judges to fast-track deportation cases for minors and blocking their access to lawyers who might help them apply for several forms of relief from removal – including acting as witnesses in cases of human trafficking or domestic violence. “By arresting and deporting survivors who have come forward and applied for protection, the Administration not only risks endangering the survivor and their family members, but the Government also sends a chilling message to the larger community: don’t call the police, don’t report crime – you or your loved ones will get deported,” reads a Wednesday letter to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from 10 current and former prosecutors. “This undermines public safety for us all.” Although Kamala Harris did not announce whether she would run for president in 2028, she did appear to signal a policy platform at the conference, saying: “We need to revisit the point of expanding the court to 13 justices like we have 13 district courts. We need to revisit, if they so want, statehood for Puerto Rico and DC.” Kamala Harris also condemned Donald Trump’s decision to enter a war with Iran, saying: “I would have opposed it even if [Congress] had approved this war.” “They’re asking for hundreds of billions of dollars to pay for this war, meanwhile, you have people in America who are losing their health care every day, cannot afford their housing, cannot afford health care, cannot afford child care. There has been no articulation of the end game,” she said. Harris went on to say: “[Trump] is now talking about this deal. You know, the deal would basically be what Barack Obama got – that he pulled us out of,” referring to the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action the US signed during the Obama administration which Trump pulled out of in 2018. “I think that it is important to not be a conspiracist, but at the same time, you can listen to what people are saying. And one, it just a full-on distraction from the things he can’t handle or has not handled. But this war is a war of choice that this president got into with Israel, with no clear national security issue,” she continued. Kamala Harris, who is speaking at the National Urban League conference in Nashville, Tennessee, said that she has “not made a decision” on a potential 2028 presidential run. “I am fully, sincerely, focused on these midterms,” she told the audience. Harris further stressed the importance of “having an agenda that is about turning out the vote in the greatest numbers we have ever seen so that…in this environment where they are cheating, we will be too big to rig.” “It means being ruthless. They are ruthless. We need to be ruthless, too. And by that, I do not mean cruel. That is not our nature. By that, I do not mean breaking the law. That is not what we do. But I do mean we must be uncompromising,” she added. Gavin Newsom and his wife made from $1.7m to $2m annually from 2022 through 2024, and paid about half a million a year in federal and state taxes, according to tax returns released by his office. The California Democratic governor’s office released more than 700 pages of tax filings spanning four years for reporters to review, offering a window into Newsom’s finances as he prepares to leave office and considers a 2028 presidential bid. Newsom’s office did not release returns for 2025, because the couple filed for an extension and will complete those returns in October. The returns show the Newsoms’ income has remained relatively consistent since he took office in 2019, when the couple reported $1.7m in annual income. The exception was in 2021, when the family sold a house for nearly $6m in Marin county, making roughly $800,000 from the sale. That year, they made $4.2m and paid more than $1m in federal and state taxes. They earned roughly $2m in 2022. The release of the couple’s tax filings comes as their finances have been under scrutiny after the US justice department launched investigations into the Newsoms, the governor announced last month. Newsom has blasted the investigations as politically motivated. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez talked about her involvement in midterm primaries and how voters are responding to the schisms in the Democratic party after the 2024 loss, which are playing out in campaigns in swing states now. She told the Majority Report this week that her motivation is “winning” and that requires “a lot of different players on the field”. When she first got to Congress, and still now, she said, there was a concrete idea in the Democratic party of who could win a swing seat, and it was “very conservative” and “very cookie-cutter”. Ocasio-Cortez is supporting Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive candidate in the US senate primary in Michigan. She has used her fundraising prowess to help candidates who were willing “to take a risk and buck convention” to help build the left movement, she said. “The reckoning that we’re seeing in some of these primaries is that what is different between Trump 1 and Trump 2 is that I think your median Democratic voter desperately wants to do everything to get Trump out of power and get Republicans out of power,” she said. “And in Trump 1, they trusted the establishment to do that. And in Trump 2, they do not. And we are seeing how that is playing out in real time.” New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said she has been surprised by polls showing her strength as a presidential candidate in 2028, saying that in her travels around the US, “people are pissed off” at the state of the country. Ocasio-Cortez appeared on leftwing podcast the Majority Report this week and shared how the electorate and politics have changed in the eight years she has served in congress. She said on data centers, in particular, a cross-partisan group is standing against them, giving Democrats a chance to harness the issue in a “majoritarian” way. “I think we always have to be making three arguments at the same time for any issue: moral argument, an economic argument, and also a political argument.
